findings.uniquenessBasis: No ledger entry, at any entryPoint, covers clean:local or the lifecycle of the generated .ts artifacts. Nearest neighbour is 4c3e1fb7f2d3 (extract-addresses.js strips a leading "Mock" with no collision guard), which concerns how the .ts files are WRITTEN; this concerns whether they are DELETED. Different mechanism, different file, different fix (add two paths to an rm list vs. add a collision guard to a rename). Kept separate.
findings.description: `clean:local` is `rm -rf broadcast/*/31337 server/deployments/progress.31337.json server/deployments/local.json && rm -rf ~/.foundry/anvil/tmp/*`. It does NOT delete `server/deployments/addresses.ts` or `server/deployments/local-addresses.ts` — the two TypeScript artifacts the external UI repo actually imports. On any chain that aborts after the clean (and the clean runs first in both job 1 and again inside `deploy:local`), the workspace is left with NO JSON and STALE TypeScript. Demonstrated empirically: after running `clean:local` against a completed deployment, `progress.31337.json` and `local.json` were gone and `broadcast/DeployMocks.s.sol/31337` was removed, while `local-addresses.ts` was byte-identical (sha256 prefix c8e0355fbc73, unchanged) and still named `PhlimboV3: "0xC32609C91d6B6b51D48f2611308FEf121B02041f"`. The asymmetry is the finding, and it runs the wrong way round: the JSON consumers inside this repo fail LOUDLY and correctly — `server/index.js` re-reads both files on every request, so `/health` honestly flipped to `deploymentsLoaded:false` and `/contracts` returned HTTP 404 — but the TypeScript consumer, which is the external UI repo and therefore the entire point of stated purpose (b), has no staleness signal whatsoever. It simply imports addresses for contracts that no longer exist on any chain.
findings.impact: A developer whose `npm run dev` aborted mid-chain, or who re-cleaned without redeploying, has a UI that builds and runs against addresses from a previous anvil session. On a fresh anvil those addresses are code-less; on a re-run they are frequently the same deterministic CREATE addresses for a DIFFERENT deployment generation, which is worse — the UI appears to work while reading a contract that is not the one it thinks it is. This is the concealment case the local-testing framing does not excuse.
findings.evidence: evidence/clean-local-stale-ts-demo.log (before/after sha256 of all four artifacts, plus the /health and /contracts responses)
findings.recommendation: Add `server/deployments/addresses.ts server/deployments/local-addresses.ts` to the `clean:local` rm list, so an aborted run leaves nothing rather than something stale. If the .ts files must survive for editor tooling, instead have `generate:ts-anvil` stamp a run id (block hash or timestamp) into both files and have the UI bootstrap assert it against `GET /health` — but deletion is simpler and fails in the safe direction.

findings.title: `dev` rehearses the cutover's end state but not its cutover mechanics: setDispatcher, replaceDispatcher and hook.pull() are executed zero times
findings.severityNote: Proposed Low. Under strict C4 a rehearsal-coverage gap is QA/Low — no deployed code is defective and no assets are at risk. It is filed prominently because the requester's stated purpose (a) is exactly 'test the whole sequence of cutovers', and this is the headline defect against it.
findings.uniquenessBasis: Two ledger entries touch rehearsal coverage and BOTH were checked and rejected as merges. c76a8f9f9479 (L-06, 'DeployMocks asserts none of story 073's headline stream state; the one probe that covers it is vacuous') is MissingPostStepAssertion — the calls ARE made, the assertions are missing, and the fix is to add requires around existing stream state. 1b461cb4d56c (L-07, test:balancer-donation ticked as the index-4 regression test but cannot exercise the streamer) is a checklist-vs-capability mismatch in a sibling npm script. This finding is structurally different: the dispatcher-repoint calls are executed ZERO times, so there is no state to assert on, and the fix is to add a whole new Phase 7.6 that performs a genuine repoint. Different root cause, different fix, kept separate. Adding assertions to L-06's stream state would not move this finding at all.
findings.description: `DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol` calls `setDispatcher` 9 times, `replaceDispatcher` 9 times and `hook.pull()` at least 3 times. `DeployMocks.s.sol` calls each of them ZERO times. Verified on the live chain: `NFTMinterV2.nextIndex == 8` with `configs[1..7]` each populated exactly once and never repointed — the local chain deploys the post-cutover dispatcher set greenfield, because it has no incumbent to displace. The mainnet script documents the per-index order at `:145-156` — `hook.pull() -> hook.setDispatcher(new) -> new.setHook(hook) -> replaceDispatcher(idx, new)` — and states in its own words that the reverse order 'would put the new dispatcher live on the index while it still carried the fresh DefaultDispatchHook that ATokenDispatcherV2's constructor gave it, so mints would SUCCEED while accruing no mint debt — a silent value leak. Never do that.' The one ordering in the whole cutover whose wrong direction is SILENT rather than loud is the one the local mirror never executes. The same omission also means these mainnet claims are never exercised locally: that `replaceDispatcher` preserves `price`/`growthBasisPoints` (asserted at `:1366-1372` and `:1536`); that `NudgeRatchet._dispatch`'s `hookTypeId() == EXPECTED_HOOK_TYPE_ID` guard holds across a hook reuse; and that `NudgeRatchetMintDebtHook`'s non-default `DEFAULT_RATIO == 100` is not silently reset. Two adjacent cutover behaviours are likewise absent with no analogue: old-batch-minter retirement (`setPauser(OWNER)` + `pause()`), and the story-074 write-once BPT custody baseline / resume-leg handling — the latter structurally un-rehearsable because `DeployMocks` writes `deploymentStatus: "completed"` unconditionally and can never record `in_progress` or `failed`.
findings.impact: A reordering regression in the mainnet cutover script — the exact defect class the mainnet script's own comment flags as a silent value leak — would pass the local rehearsal unchanged, because the local rehearsal contains none of the calls involved. The rehearsal's green result therefore carries less assurance than it appears to, which is the concealment bar. No claim is made that the mainnet ordering IS wrong; the finding is that `dev` cannot tell you either way.
findings.evidence: grep counts over both scripts (setDispatcher 0 vs 9, replaceDispatcher 0 vs 9); evidence/cast-live-state.log (NFTMinterV2 nextIndex=8, configs[1..7] all greenfield); evidence/dev-script-narrative.log (25 phases, none of them a repoint); reports/.../script-audits/dev/cluster-analysis.md G-1/G-2/G-3

findings.title: The local chain arms a Kendu promotion that story 076 asserts must be dormant on mainnet, and never produces the dormant state the UI will actually ship against
findings.uniquenessBasis: The only Kendu-bearing ledger entry is acabc052baaa (L-09, whitelisting Kendu on the shared batch minter with vacuous/undone fee-on-transfer evidence) — a token-configuration and evidence-quality finding on a different contract with a different fix. findings.description: `_armLocalKenduPromotion` arms a 10,000-Kendu / 1-day promotion on PhlimboV3. Verified live: `promoToken == MockKendu`, `promoPhase == Active (1)`, `promoRewardBalance == 10,000e18`, `promoRewardPerSecond == 1.157e35`. Story 076 asserts the exact opposite for mainnet — `promoToken == address(0)`, Kendu deliberately unset, Phase 7 asserting the negative — and `DeployMainnetPromotionReady.s.sol` calls `startPromotion` nowhere. THE ARMING ITSELF IS ADMISSIBLE and is not the finding: it is declared deliberate at `:183-198`, argued well (with no promotion running, every new V3 UI field — 13/16/17/18/19 plus the three unclaimable banks on DepositPageViewV3 — reads zero, which is indistinguishable from a broken binding), and carefully sequenced dead-last so the migrator's `promoToken`-delta path stays dormant during the migration. The finding is the INVERSE: because the promotion is armed unconditionally at the end of every local run, no local run ever produces the DORMANT promo state that mainnet will actually ship on day one. The UI's dormant-promotion rendering path is the one path `dev` never exercises, and it is the path that goes live first. Compounding it, `mainnet-addresses.ts` carries `Kendu: "0x000…0"` (see ledger 3177eed94ecb), so a UI developer working against `dev` sees an active promotion on a live Kendu token where mainnet will present a dormant promotion on the zero address. Note per project policy that the in-source comment declaring this deliberate is evidence of intent, not suppression authority.
findings.impact: The day-one mainnet UI state — dormant promo, zero-address Kendu — is the single state the local rehearsal cannot produce, so any rendering bug specific to it (a zero-division on `promoRewardPerSecond`, a null-token symbol lookup, a banner that renders 'promotion active' off a non-zero `promoPhase` enum) ships unrehearsed. This is a purpose-(b) blind spot created by an otherwise-sound purpose-(b) shortcut.

findings.recommendation: Make both promo states reachable locally. Either way, keep the four non-vacuous post-condition requires — they are correct and should not be relaxed.

findings.title: The deploy script grants itself phUSD mint authority and never revokes it, while correctly revoking PhlimboV2's grant in the same run
findings.uniquenessBasis: No prior entry at any entryPoint concerns residual deployer privilege or phUSD minter ACL end-state. The two ACL-adjacent dev entries (c294d93f772b pauser==0, 0b497be32114 migrator==0) are missing-constructor-argument findings on StableStaker, not un-revoked grants on the phUSD token. Distinct mechanism, distinct fix. Unique.
findings.description: `phUSD.setMinter(deployer, true)` is granted at `:1784`, `:2025` and `:2122` and is never revoked. Verified live at the end of the run: `phUSD.authorizedMinters(0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266) == (true, 1)`. The grant is a legitimate local shortcut — the deployer acts as a synthetic donor to seed the phUSD nudge stream, which story 073 sanctions — and the token is a mock on a chain whose keys are public, so there is no local risk. The finding is the inconsistency and what it costs the rehearsal: the SAME script, in the SAME run, correctly revokes PhlimboV2's grant as an explicit ordered step of the Phase 7.4 wind-down (verified: `authorizedMinters(PhlimboV2) == (false, 1)`, `authorizedMinters(PhlimboV3) == (true, 1)`), and logs it as such. So privilege revocation is clearly understood as a first-class cutover step here — just not applied to the deployer's own grant. Consequently the local chain's end state carries a live minter that mainnet's end state must not, and the 'revoke the operational key's temporary grant' step is never rehearsed even though it is precisely the kind of step that is easy to forget on a Ledger broadcast.
findings.impact: No local risk (mock token, public anvil key). The cost is rehearsal fidelity: a residual-privilege sweep is never exercised, and the local end state differs from the intended mainnet end state in a way no assertion catches. This is an owner footgun of the non-obvious kind — the script's own careful revocation of the OTHER grant makes it read as though residual privileges were swept.
findings.lawNote: Law 3: filed as a non-obvious owner footgun, not a malicious-owner vector. The surprise test is met — a competent operator reading the Phase 7.4 wind-down would reasonably conclude the ACL was swept.
findings.recommendation: Revoke the deployer's grant at the end of `run()` with `phUSD.setMinter(deployer, false)` and assert it, mirroring the Phase 7.4 wind-down's own pattern. Better still, add a terminal 'residual privilege sweep' phase that asserts the full expected end-state ACL — deployer not a minter, PhlimboV2 not a minter, PhlimboV3 a minter — so the check is declarative and a future grant that forgets to clean up fails the run.

Under Law 1 an untested destructive branch in a script that rm -rf's a shared user directory it does not own must stay visible; under the project's no-speculation rule it must not be filed as a finding on an undemonstrated consequence. Parking is the correct third option and it stands. The resolution step is cheap and decisive and should be run: start a second `anvil --fork-url $RPC_MAINNET --state <dir>` alongside, run clean:local, observe. The sanitizer added nothing new to manual-review.json, so the file is unchanged.
